4: Conclusion: Israel Remains Israel; the Body Remains the Body

The passages examined distinguish Israel and the Body of Christ by the names, covenants, promises, relationships, and expectations they explicitly assign to each. Peter describes the prophetic hope as that which God had “spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began” (Acts 3:21), while Paul describes the mystery as having been “kept secret since the world began” (Romans 16:25). Israel is identified as a nation with its origin in the promises to Abraham (Exodus 19:6; Romans 9:4–5), while Paul identifies the church as Christ’s Body, with Christ as its head (Ephesians 1:22–23). Israel’s covenants are named with the house of Israel and the house of Judah (Jeremiah 31:31), while Gentiles are described as formerly “strangers from the covenants of promise” and then “made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:12–13). Israel’s passages speak of land, restoration, Jerusalem, and David’s throne; Paul describes believers as blessed “in heavenly places in Christ,” as displaying God’s wisdom through the church, and as awaiting their gathering to Christ and appearing with Him in glory (Ephesians 1:3; 3:10; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Colossians 3:4). Taken together, these passages continue to identify Israel according to Israel’s stated national and covenantal promises and the church as Christ’s Body with the heavenly standing and hope Paul describes.
5: Conclusion: Complete in the Calling God Has Given the Body

The passages examined describe a consistent heavenly pattern for the Body of Christ. Paul identifies the church as Christ’s Body with Christ as its Head (Ephesians 1:22–23), describes believers as raised and seated together “in heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6), and says they are blessed with “all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1:3). He identifies their citizenship as being in heaven, from which they await the Savior and the transformation of their bodies (Philippians 3:20–21), while Colossians describes their life as presently hidden with Christ and their future as appearing with Him in glory (Colossians 3:3–4). First Thessalonians 4:16–17 adds the resurrection of the dead in Christ, the catching up of living believers, and their enduring presence with the Lord. Ephesians further places the church’s spiritual conflict and the display of God’s manifold wisdom within the heavenly sphere (Ephesians 3:10; 6:12). These passages describe a present position as well as a future manifestation, and they do not reduce the heavenly calling merely to a future destination. Taken together, these passages present the Body’s heavenly calling as a Christ-centered identity, position, blessing, citizenship, hope, conflict, and purpose grounded in union with Christ.
6: Study 6: The Mystery Revealed Through Paul
Conclusion: God’s Previously Hidden Purpose in Christ

The passages examined define the Mystery by its revelatory history: it was “kept secret since the world began,” “hid in God,” and “hid from ages and from generations,” but was subsequently revealed (Romans 16:25; Ephesians 3:9; Colossians 1:26). Paul states that he received his message by revelation from Jesus Christ and that the Mystery was made known to him by revelation (Galatians 1:12; Ephesians 3:3), while Ephesians 3:5 also states that it was revealed by the Spirit to holy apostles and prophets. Ephesians identifies Jew and Gentile as fellow heirs and members of “the same body,” reconciled to God in one Body through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16; 3:6), while Paul describes that Body as blessed and seated in heavenly places in Christ (Ephesians 1:3; 2:6). Colossians adds “Christ in you, the hope of glory,” and 1 Corinthians 15 identifies the transformation of living believers as a mystery (Colossians 1:27; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52). Ephesians 3:10 further states that through the church God’s manifold wisdom is made known to principalities and powers in heavenly places. These statements stand in contrast to the prophetic revelation Peter describes as that which God had spoken through His prophets since the world began (Acts 3:21). Taken together, these passages present the Mystery as a previously hidden purpose of God in Christ, revealed through Paul, concerning the one Body and its union with Christ, heavenly position, hope, and place in God’s revealed purpose.
7: Study 7: The Day of the Lord
Conclusion: Keep the Day and the Hope Distinct

The passages examined describe the Day of the Lord within the prophetic Scriptures as a time of divine intervention marked by wrath, darkness, judgment, cosmic disturbance, and judgment involving Israel and the nations (Isaiah 13:6–13; Joel 2:1–11; Amos 5:18–20; Zephaniah 1:14–18). Zechariah 14 places the Lord’s visible intervention within that prophetic setting and describes His feet standing upon the Mount of Olives, while the larger prophetic record moves from judgment toward deliverance, restoration, and Messiah’s reign. Paul likewise says that the Day comes “as a thief in the night” and that sudden destruction comes upon “them,” but immediately distinguishes his readers as “brethren” who are “not in darkness” and are “not appointed...to wrath” (1 Thessalonians 5:2–9). In the preceding passage, Paul describes the dead in Christ rising and living believers being caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air and “ever be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). He also describes Jesus as the One who delivers believers “from the wrath to come” (1 Thessalonians 1:10). The interpretation of details in 2 Thessalonians 2, including the textual variation concerning “the day of Christ” or “the day of the Lord” and questions surrounding the chapter’s chronology, remains disputed; the findings above do not depend upon resolving those questions. Taken together, these passages present the Day of the Lord within Israel’s prophetic setting of judgment moving toward restoration, while Paul presents believers as awaiting their gathering to Christ and as not appointed to the wrath associated with the coming Day.
8: Conclusion: Completion, Accountability, Glory, and Christ

The passages examined explicitly associate the Day of Christ with God’s continuing work toward completion, sincerity and blamelessness, confidence unto the end, and future rejoicing concerning faithful labor. Philippians 1:6 states that God will perform the good work He began until the Day of Jesus Christ; Philippians 1:10 directs believers toward sincerity and being without offence until the Day of Christ; Philippians 2:16 connects that Day with Paul’s rejoicing concerning his labor; and 1 Corinthians 1:8 speaks of confirmation unto the end and blamelessness in the Day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Other Pauline passages separately describe the Body’s future gathering to Christ, resurrection and transformation, appearance with Christ in glory, accountability before the Judgment Seat of Christ, and presentation of the church to Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52; Colossians 3:4; Romans 14:10; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Ephesians 5:27). These related doctrines contribute to the larger Pauline hope but are not individually called the Day of Christ in the passages that establish them. The wording of 2 Thessalonians 2:2 remains disputed between “day of Christ” and “day of the Lord,” and the conclusions above do not depend upon resolving that textual question. Taken together, these passages present the Day of Christ as a future Christ-centered horizon of completion, blamelessness, confidence, and rejoicing, within the larger Pauline hope of gathering, transformation, accountability, presentation, and glory with Christ.
9: The passages examined present the remnant within Israel as evidence of God’s preserving faithfulness amid unbelief and judgment. In Elijah’s day, God preserved seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18), and the prophets repeatedly describe a remnant preserved within Israel through judgment (Isaiah 10:20–22; Jeremiah 23:3). Paul applies that pattern directly in Romans 11, where he asks whether God has cast away His people, answers “God forbid,” identifies himself as an Israelite, and states that “at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:1–5). The remnant therefore remains a remnant of the people Paul continues to identify as Israel; its preservation does not create a new national identity. Romans 11 also distinguishes Israel and Gentiles in the olive-tree illustration and warns Gentiles against boasting, while Revelation 7 continues to identify the 144,000 according to the tribes of Israel. The remnant does not make God faithful; its preservation bears witness to the faithfulness of the God who has not cast away His people. Taken together, these passages present Israel’s remnant as a preserved believing portion within Israel through which judgment does not erase Israel’s identity or overturn God’s continuing purpose concerning the people He names as His own.
10: Conclusion: God’s Faithfulness to His Prophetic Word

The passages examined place Daniel’s seventy-week prophecy upon Daniel’s people and holy city, Israel and Jerusalem (Daniel 9:24). Daniel divides the prophecy so that sixty-nine weeks lead to Messiah, after which Messiah is cut off and the city and sanctuary are destroyed, while verse 27 describes a remaining final week (Daniel 9:25–27). Within that week, Daniel identifies a covenant confirmed with many, the continuation of sacrifice and offering, and a midpoint at which those sacrifices cease and desolation comes into view. Jesus later directs His hearers to Daniel’s abomination of desolation and states that great tribulation follows it, placing the Great Tribulation after the midpoint rather than making it synonymous with the entire seventieth week (Matthew 24:15–21). Scripture elsewhere uses corresponding three-and-one-half-year expressions that contribute to the prophetic description of this latter period, while Matthew 24 moves from the tribulation to the visible appearing of the Son of Man (Matthew 24:29–31). The prophecy consistently retains Israel and Jerusalem as its stated setting; the Body of Christ is not named as a subject of Daniel’s seventy weeks. Taken together, these passages present Daniel’s seventieth week as the remaining final period of the seventy-week prophecy determined upon Israel and Jerusalem, moving through its marked midpoint and Great Tribulation toward Messiah’s appearing and the fulfillment of God’s prophetic purpose concerning Israel.
11: Study 11: The Beginning of the Body of Christ
Conclusion: The Body Begins with Paul at Acts 9

The passages examined distinguish the believing assemblies already present within Israel’s prophetic setting from the Church Paul identifies as Christ’s Body. At Pentecost, Peter addresses Israel, explains the Spirit’s outpouring from Joel, appeals to the Davidic promise, and proclaims Jesus as Israel’s risen Lord and Christ (Acts 2:14–36). The use of ekklesia does not by itself establish Body identity, since Scripture uses the term for different kinds of assemblies (Acts 7:38; 19:32, 39, 41). Paul, by contrast, identifies the church as Christ’s Body and describes the one Body as belonging to the Mystery that had previously been hidden and was made known through his distinctive stewardship (Ephesians 1:22–23; 3:2–6; Colossians 1:18, 26). Acts 9 records Paul’s historical calling by the risen Christ, while Galatians 1:11–17 establishes the independent revelatory source of his gospel and Ephesians 3:2–3 identifies the stewardship and Mystery made known to him. First Timothy 1:16 further describes Paul’s salvation in pattern-setting terms, although the verse does not explicitly call him the first member of the Body. Acts 9 itself does not state that “the Body began today”; that conclusion arises cumulatively from Paul’s calling and his later inspired explanation of the Mystery entrusted through him. Taken together, these passages place the historical beginning of the Church which is Christ’s Body with Paul’s Acts 9 calling and the beginning of the previously hidden Mystery Program, while Israel’s Prophecy Program continues alongside it through the Acts overlap.
12: Conclusion: What Is the New Covenant?

The passages examined identify the house of Israel and the house of Judah as the parties of the New Covenant and describe the covenant as God’s promised transformation and restoration of that people. Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises the law written within, restored relationship with God, knowledge of the LORD, and forgiveness, while Ezekiel 36:24–28 describes cleansing, a new heart and spirit, God’s Spirit within the restored people, regathering, and return to the land. These provisions do not originate Israel’s nationhood, land, King, throne, or Kingdom, since the Abrahamic and Davidic promises establishing those features precede the New Covenant (Genesis 12:1–3; 2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus identifies His blood with the New Covenant, establishing His sacrificial death as the redemptive basis of its fulfillment (Luke 22:20). Romans 11:26–29 continues to connect Israel’s future deliverance with covenant promise, and Romans 9:4 associates the covenants with Israel. Paul’s statement that he is an able minister of the New Covenant in 2 Corinthians 3:6 describes his ministry but does not identify the Body of Christ as the house of Israel, the house of Judah, or a named covenant party. Taken together, these passages present the New Covenant as God’s promised forgiveness, inward transformation, restored relationship, and spiritual restoration of Israel and Judah, secured through Christ’s blood and brought to fulfillment within God’s prophetic purpose for Israel.
13: Study 13: The Olive Tree and the Body of Christ

The passages examined present the olive-tree illustration within Paul’s discussion of Israel’s unbelief, Gentile blessing, and God’s continuing purpose for Israel. Romans 11 begins with Paul denying that God has cast away His people, and Paul immediately identifies himself as an Israelite while describing a remnant within Israel (Romans 11:1–5). In the illustration, Israel is represented by natural branches, some of which are broken off because of unbelief, while a wild olive branch is grafted in among them and becomes a partaker of the root and fatness of the olive tree (Romans 11:17–20). Paul continues to distinguish the wild branch from the natural branches after grafting and states that broken natural branches may be grafted into “their own olive tree” again (Romans 11:23–24). The illustration therefore changes the standing and participation of the branches without describing a change in their underlying identity. Romans 11:25–29 continues to call the nation Israel and grounds its future in God’s faithfulness and His relationship to the fathers. When Paul explains the Body of Christ elsewhere, he uses different language: believing Jew and Gentile are made one new man and reconciled to God in one Body in Christ (Ephesians 2:13–16). Taken together, these passages present the olive tree as an illustration of participation in Abrahamic-rooted prophetic blessing and standing, while the one Body describes the distinct Mystery identity God creates in Christ; grafting changes participation, not identity.
14: The passages examined establish Acts 9 as a genuine beginning without presenting it as the immediate termination of what was already operating. Acts 1–8 remains centered upon Israel, Jerusalem, the Twelve, prophetic fulfillment, signs, repentance, restoration, and the promised Kingdom. In Acts 9, the risen Christ personally confronts Saul and identifies him as a chosen vessel who will bear His name before Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel (Acts 9:3–15). Paul later states that his gospel came through revelation of Jesus Christ rather than from human instruction and that he did not immediately go to the apostles before him (Galatians 1:11–17), while his later epistles identify the Mystery and stewardship made known through him. Yet Acts itself shows that Peter’s ministry continues after Saul’s calling: Peter heals Aeneas and raises Dorcas in the same chapter, remains prominent in Acts 10–12, and participates in the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15. Paul also repeatedly encounters Jewish audiences throughout his Acts ministry, demonstrating that Israel’s prophetic setting remains historically present after Acts 9. Acts 28 later records Paul’s application of Isaiah’s judicial-blinding language and his declaration that the salvation of God is sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:25–28). Taken together, these passages establish Acts 9 as the historical beginning of Paul’s distinctive apostleship and the Mystery Program while Israel’s Prophecy Program continues, producing the concurrent operation of Prophecy and Mystery until the later Acts 28 suspension point.
16: Study 16: The Believer’s Identity in Christ
Conclusion: Live From the Identity God Has Given

The passages examined locate the believer’s identity in what God has accomplished in Christ rather than in what the believer achieves through performance. Ephesians describes believers as blessed, chosen, accepted, redeemed, and sealed in relation to Christ (Ephesians 1:3–14), while Romans 6, Galatians 2:20, and Colossians 3:1–4 identify believers with Christ’s death and life and describe their present life as hidden with Christ in God. Second Corinthians 5:17 identifies the person in Christ as a new creation, while 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 describes believers as members of one Body formed by the Spirit, with Ephesians and Colossians identifying Christ as its Head. Paul further describes believers as complete in Christ, sealed by the Spirit, raised and seated together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus, and possessing heavenly citizenship (Colossians 2:10; Ephesians 1:13–14; 2:6; Philippians 3:20). These positional statements precede and ground Paul’s commands concerning the believer’s walk: Ephesians first establishes what God has accomplished and then calls believers to “walk worthy,” while Colossians grounds its commands in the realities already stated concerning life with Christ (Ephesians 4:1; Colossians 3:1–5). Taken together, these passages present Christian identity as a God-given standing in Christ that includes new creation, membership in one Body, acceptance, completeness, spiritual sealing, and heavenly position, from which the believer’s conduct is then called to proceed.
17: Conclusion: Let the Covenant Keep Its Biblical Shape

The passages examined present the Abrahamic Covenant as a coordinated set of divine promises concerning Abraham, his covenant line, nationhood, land, and blessing extending to the nations. Genesis 12:1–7 promises that Abraham will become a great nation, that God will bless him, that blessing will extend to all families of the earth through him, and that the land will be given to his seed. Genesis 13, 15, and 17 progressively specify the land and its enduring connection with Abraham’s seed. In the ratification scene of Genesis 15, Abraham is placed in a deep sleep while the divine manifestation passes between the divided pieces, and the text states that the LORD made the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15:12–18). Genesis 17 then distinguishes blessing upon Ishmael from the covenant specifically established with Isaac, and subsequent passages carry the promise through Isaac to Jacob, whom God names Israel (Genesis 17:18–21; 26:3–4; 28:13–14). The same Genesis passages repeatedly extend blessing to the nations without describing the nations as replacing the covenant line or becoming Israel. The Abrahamic promises also precede the Mosaic Covenant, and Leviticus 26:42–44 explicitly recalls God’s covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob even in the setting of Israel’s covenant judgment. Taken together, these passages present the Abrahamic Covenant as God’s pledged purpose concerning Abraham and the covenant line leading through Isaac and Jacob to Israel, including nation, land, seed, and an outward extension of blessing to the nations without erasing the identity of the covenant recipients.
18: Conclusion: Distinct Commissions Within One Divine Purpose

The passages examined present Peter and Paul as servants of the same Lord who were entrusted with distinguishable apostolic commissions. Jesus sends the Twelve to the lost sheep of the house of Israel with the Kingdom proclamation and promises them twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 10:5–7; 19:28). Peter’s early Acts ministry continues in that identified setting as he addresses Judaea, Israel, and the house of Israel and speaks to those he calls children of the prophets and of the covenant (Acts 2:14, 22, 36; 3:25). Paul is called separately by the risen Christ as a chosen vessel whose ministry will extend to Gentiles, kings, and Israel, and Paul states that his apostleship and gospel came through Jesus Christ rather than from human appointment or instruction (Acts 9:15; Galatians 1:1, 11–12). In Galatians 2, the Jerusalem leaders add nothing to Paul, distinguish what was committed to Paul from what was committed to Peter, recognize God’s activity in both ministries, and extend the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:6–9). Peter later refers to Paul as “our beloved brother,” demonstrating that distinction between their ministries does not itself require hostility (2 Peter 3:15–16). Taken together, these passages present Peter’s apostleship within Israel’s prophetic and Kingdom commission and Paul’s apostleship as a distinct commission received from the risen Christ and associated with the Mystery, while showing that recognition and fellowship between the apostles did not require their commissions to become identical.
19: The passages examined show that the Jerusalem Council addressed a specific controversy over whether Gentile believers were required to be circumcised and commanded to keep the Law of Moses (Acts 15:1–5). Peter responds by recalling how God had already caused Gentiles to hear and believe, had given them the Holy Spirit, and had purified their hearts by faith; he therefore opposes placing the Mosaic yoke upon the Gentile disciples (Acts 15:7–11). Paul and Barnabas then report the work God had already accomplished among the Gentiles through their ministry (Acts 15:12). James appeals to the prophets and cites Amos concerning David’s fallen tabernacle and Gentiles called by the Lord’s name, showing that Gentile blessing agrees with Israel’s prophetic Scriptures without identifying Amos as a revelation of the previously hidden Body of Christ (Acts 15:13–18). James’s judgment is that the Gentiles turning to God should not be troubled with the disputed Mosaic requirements, and the resulting letter explicitly states that those demanding circumcision and Law keeping had received no such commandment from Jerusalem (Acts 15:19–29). Galatians 2:6–9 likewise records recognition of distinguishable responsibilities committed to Peter and Paul together with fellowship between their representatives. Taken together, these passages present the Jerusalem Council as recognition of God’s work among the Gentiles and a rejection of circumcision and Mosaic Law keeping as requirements for their standing before God, while preserving the distinguishable apostolic ministries already operating during the Acts overlap.
20: The passages examined place Acts 2:38 within Peter’s Pentecostal address to Israel and the prophetic setting Peter himself establishes. Peter addresses “men of Judaea,” “men of Israel,” and “all the house of Israel,” explains the Spirit’s outpouring through Joel, appeals to Davidic prophecy, and identifies the crucified and risen Jesus as Lord and Christ (Acts 2:14–36). After Peter’s hearers are pricked in their hearts and ask what they should do, Peter commands them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins and promises the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:37–39). The passage therefore presents repentance and water baptism as commanded elements of Peter’s answer to the Israelite audience standing before him; it does not present physical water as the meritorious ground of forgiveness. Acts 3:19–21 continues the same apostolic setting by calling Israel to repentance in connection with sins being blotted out, times of refreshing, and the restitution of all things spoken through the prophets. Paul later describes a different baptism in connection with the Body, stating that believers are baptized by one Spirit into one Body and identifying “one baptism” within that corporate calling (1 Corinthians 12:13; Ephesians 4:4–5). Taken together, these passages present Acts 2:38 as Peter’s commanded response to Israel in the Pentecostal Prophecy and Kingdom setting, while Paul’s one-Body teaching identifies Spirit incorporation as the baptism associated with the Body of Christ.
21: Conclusion: A Judicial Suspension, Not a Covenant Cancellation

The passages examined distinguish Israel’s persistent unbelief and hardening from the later national judicial boundary recorded at the close of Acts. Isaiah 6:9–10 supplies the prophetic language of hearing without understanding and seeing without perceiving, language later applied in the Gospels to Israel’s resistance without those earlier citations themselves ending Israel’s prophetic administration. Early Acts continues to address Israel with repentance, restoration, and prophetic hope, and the beginning of Paul’s ministry at Acts 9 occurs while that Israelward testimony remains active. Romans 11 states that God has not cast away His people, identifies a remnant according to grace, describes Israel’s blindness as “in part,” places an “until” boundary upon it, and affirms Israel’s future salvation along with the continuing gifts and calling of God (Romans 11:1–5, 25–29). At Rome, Paul addresses Jewish leaders concerning “the hope of Israel,” reasons from Moses and the prophets, encounters a divided response, then applies Isaiah’s hardening language and declares that the salvation of God is sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:17–28). Taken together, these passages present Acts 28 as the national judicial suspension of Israel’s active Prophecy administration, while Israel’s identity, covenants, calling, and promised future remain intact for their future prophetic fulfillment.
22: Conclusion: Prayer With Confidence Under Grace

The passages examined show that prayer continues under Grace while the promises governing prayer must be identified by their audience and revealed setting. Jesus’ statements concerning asking and receiving in Matthew 7:7–11, Matthew 21:21–22, Mark 11:22–24, and John 14–16 are spoken within the Kingdom and apostolic settings in which those promises were given. Paul’s instructions to the Body emphasize continual prayer, supplication, thanksgiving, intercession, watchfulness, perseverance, and prayer for the progress of ministry (1 Thessalonians 5:17; Ephesians 6:18–20; Colossians 4:2–4; 1 Timothy 2:1–2). Philippians 4:6–7 directs believers to make their requests known to God with thanksgiving and promises the guarding peace of God, while Romans 8:26–27 describes the Spirit helping believers in weakness when they do not know what to pray for. Paul himself asked repeatedly for his thorn to depart, yet the answer he received was, “My grace is sufficient for thee” (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). His recorded prayers also emphasize wisdom, spiritual understanding, strengthening, love, discernment, fruitful conduct, and effective ministry. Taken together, these passages present prayer under Grace as continual, thankful, intercessory, request-making dependence upon God, accompanied by the Spirit’s help and God’s sufficient grace without turning every requested circumstantial outcome into a guaranteed promise.
23: Conclusion: A Sealed Subset Within Israel’s Remnant

The passages examined identify the 144,000 according to explicit Israelite and tribal language. Revelation 7:4 calls them 144,000 “of all the tribes of the children of Israel,” and the verses that follow assign twelve thousand to each of twelve named tribes (Revelation 7:4–8). Their sealing occurs before further judgment is released upon the earth, sea, and trees, identifying them as servants of God within Revelation’s prophetic crisis (Revelation 7:1–3). Revelation then distinguishes this numbered Israelite company from an innumerable multitude drawn from nations, kindreds, peoples, and tongues (Revelation 7:9). Revelation 14 returns to the same number and presents the 144,000 with the Lamb on Mount Sion, bearing the Father’s name in their foreheads, learning a distinctive song, following the Lamb, and being called “firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb” (Revelation 14:1–5). The broader biblical remnant category is not limited to this one numbered company, while Revelation gives the 144,000 features that distinguish them within that larger remnant. Taken together, these passages present the 144,000 as a specifically numbered, sealed, Israelite company within Israel’s broader believing remnant, distinguished from the great multitude and identified with the Lamb within Revelation’s prophetic setting.
24: Conclusion: Hold Fast Rather Than Draw Back

The passages examined identify the willful sin of Hebrews 10:26–31 through the argument surrounding the warning rather than as every deliberate moral failure. Hebrews 10:19–25 calls the hearers to draw near, hold fast their profession, remain assembled, and encourage one another as the Day approaches; verse 26 then introduces the consequence of willfully turning from received truth. Verse 29 describes that repudiation as treading underfoot the Son of God, counting the blood of the covenant an unholy thing, and insulting the Spirit of grace. The preceding sacrificial argument establishes Christ’s offering as final and once for all, so “there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins” means that repudiating Christ leaves no alternative sacrifice (Hebrews 10:1–18, 26). The comparison with one who despised Moses’ law and the quotations concerning divine vengeance place the warning within Hebrews’ covenant and judgment framework (Hebrews 10:28–31). The section closes by contrasting drawing back unto perdition with believing to the saving of the soul (Hebrews 10:38–39). Taken together, these passages present the willful sin as knowing repudiation of the Son and His final sacrifice after receiving the knowledge of the truth, and they call Hebrews’ hearers to hold fast in faith rather than draw back.
25: Conclusion: Let the Signs Remain With the Commission They Confirm

The passages examined present the signs of Mark 16:17–18 as part of the commission in which the risen Christ sends His messengers to preach. Mark 16:15–16 joins proclamation with the stated response of belief and baptism, while verses 17–18 identify accompanying signs including casting out devils, new tongues, protection in specified dangers, and healing. Mark 16:20 then states the function of the signs: the Lord worked with the messengers, “confirming the word with signs following.” Corresponding signs appear in Acts, including tongues, healings, and Paul’s preservation from the viper, while Paul separately refers to “the signs of an apostle” in connection with his ministry. Paul’s own commission and Body doctrine, however, use different controlling statements: Christ sent Paul “not to baptize, but to preach the gospel,” and Paul identifies baptism by one Spirit into one Body (1 Corinthians 1:17; 12:13). The manuscript status of Mark 16:9–20 remains a textual question, but the study’s contextual interpretation reads the passage as it stands without making that question determine its meaning. Taken together, these passages present the signs of Mark 16 as confirming signs attached to the commission in which they are given, while Paul’s later Mystery revelation identifies the Body’s commission and baptism on their own stated terms.
26: Study 26: The Seven Churches of Revelation

The passages examined identify the seven churches of Revelation as real assemblies in seven named cities addressed within a book that explicitly calls itself prophecy (Revelation 1:3–4, 11). Revelation identifies the seven lampstands as the seven churches and the seven stars as their angels, while leaving the precise nature of those angels open to interpretation (Revelation 1:20). Across the seven messages, Christ evaluates the assemblies’ works and conditions, commends faithfulness, exposes failure, commands repentance or endurance, warns of consequences, and promises rewards to those who overcome (Revelation 2–3). The promises and warnings repeatedly connect with Revelation’s larger themes of tribulation, kingdom authority, the nations, the temple, the throne, life, and the New Jerusalem. The noun ekklesia establishes that these recipients are assemblies but does not by itself identify them as the Church which is Christ’s Body, since Scripture uses the same word for different assemblies. Revelation also never states that the seven churches represent seven successive eras of later church history; that scheme remains an interpretive construction rather than an explicit statement of the text. Taken together, these passages present the seven churches as historical assemblies addressed within Revelation’s prophetic setting, accountable to Christ’s evaluation and promises, whose meaning must be established from Revelation itself before broader application is drawn.
27: The passages examined identify the seven annual appointed feasts as observances given to Israel within the Mosaic covenant and distinguish them from the weekly Sabbath that introduces Leviticus 23. Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Weeks, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Tabernacles order Israel’s worship through historical remembrance, agricultural seasons, priestly service, sacred assemblies, sacrifice, cleansing, and rejoicing. Scripture also supplies specific later connections without assigning equal certainty to every proposed prophetic correspondence: Paul explicitly identifies Christ as “our passover” and as “the firstfruits of them that slept” (1 Corinthians 5:7; 15:20), Acts 2 places Pentecost within Peter’s explanation from Joel and his address to Israel, and Zechariah 14 places Tabernacles within a future earthly kingdom setting centered upon the reigning LORD. Other proposed one-to-one correspondences involving Trumpets, Atonement, the Pentecost loaves, or exact prophetic chronologies are not stated with the same explicitness and therefore remain matters of inference or dispute. Taken together, these passages present Israel’s seven appointed feasts as covenant observances with their own historical meaning and assignment, while later Scripture reveals particular Christological and prophetic connections that deepen their significance without transferring Israel’s calendar to the Body of Christ.
28: The passages examined place Hebrews 6:4–6 within a sustained exhortation concerning maturity, received privilege, perseverance, and the danger of falling away. Hebrews 5:11–14 rebukes dullness of hearing, and Hebrews 6:1–3 calls the hearers to advance beyond foundational instruction. The warning then describes people who were enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift and the good word of God, became partakers of the Holy Ghost, and tasted the powers of the world to come before speaking of their falling away and the impossibility of renewing them again to repentance (Hebrews 6:4–6). The land illustration that follows describes ground receiving the same rain but producing either useful fruit or thorns and briers, with the latter ending in rejection, cursing, and burning (Hebrews 6:7–8). The writer then turns to “better things,” diligence, full assurance of hope, Abraham’s patient endurance, God’s unchangeable promise, and the hope anchored within the veil where Jesus has entered as High Priest (Hebrews 6:9–20). The passage does not identify these categories as Pauline descriptions of membership in the Body or use the language of the Body’s sealing and completeness in Christ. Taken together, these passages present Hebrews 6 as a real warning to privileged hearers against falling away from received revelation, followed by an equally real call to diligent perseverance grounded in God’s promise and Christ’s priesthood.
29: Study 29: One Taken and the Other Left

The passages examined place the “one taken, and the other left” sayings within the prophetic appearing of the Son of Man and the judgment comparisons supplied by Jesus. Matthew 24 locates the coming after the Tribulation and describes the visible coming of the Son of Man with power and great glory (Matthew 24:27–31). Jesus then compares that coming with the days of Noah, when ordinary activity continued until the Flood came and took away the unprepared while Noah and his household were preserved (Matthew 24:37–39). Luke 17 adds the days of Lot, again placing ordinary activity immediately before sudden destruction, and follows the separation sayings with the disciples’ question, “Where, Lord?” and Jesus’ answer concerning the body and gathered eagles (Luke 17:26–37). These contextual features support the conclusion that the person taken is removed in judgment while the person left is preserved, although neither Gospel gives that interpretation in a single explicit explanatory sentence. Paul’s gathering passages describe the Body’s hope differently, including resurrection of the dead in Christ, transformation, and meeting the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52). Taken together, Matthew 24 and Luke 17 present the taken-and-left separation as a judgment associated with the Son of Man’s prophetic appearing, with the removed person taken in judgment and the remaining person preserved, rather than as the Pauline gathering of the Body of Christ.
30: Study 30: Seated With Christ in Heavenly Places
Conclusion: Secure in Christ, Awaiting Manifestation

The passages examined present the Body’s seated position as a present, grace-given reality possessed in Christ rather than as independent authority belonging to believers apart from Him. Ephesians 1:19–23 first establishes Christ’s unique exaltation: God raised Him, seated Him at His right hand in heavenly places, placed Him far above every principality, power, might, dominion, and name, and gave Him as Head over all things to the church, which is His Body. Ephesians 2:4–7 then states that God made believers alive together with Christ, raised them together, and seated them together in heavenly places “in Christ Jesus.” The Body’s position is therefore derivative and relational, while Christ remains the exalted Head. Ephesians 3:10 states that God’s manifold wisdom is made known through the church to principalities and powers in heavenly places, while Colossians 2:10 identifies believers as complete in Christ, who is Head of all principality and power. Colossians 3:1–4 further distinguishes present hidden life with Christ from future manifestation with Him in glory, while other Pauline passages speak of judging angels, evaluation of service, reward, and reigning without supplying a complete structure of future heavenly administration. Taken together, these passages present the Body as presently raised and seated with Christ by grace, entirely in and under its exalted Head, with a position that awaits future manifestation and service without establishing present independent government over heavenly powers.
31: The passages examined present divine judgment in distinct settings with different subjects, timing, standards, purposes, and outcomes. Historical judgments such as the Flood, Babel, Sodom, Egypt, Canaan, and Israel’s covenant discipline demonstrate God’s righteous government in history, while the Cross presents Christ bearing judgment as the redemptive basis of the believer’s acceptance before God. First Corinthians 11:27–32 addresses self-examination and present discipline, whereas Romans 14:10–12, 1 Corinthians 3:8–15, and 2 Corinthians 5:9–10 describe the future evaluation of the Body’s service, where works may receive reward or suffer loss without reversing the believer’s salvation. Prophetic passages separately describe Israel’s accountability, Tribulation and Day of the Lord judgments, the judgment of living nations at the Son of Man’s return, and judgments associated with the Kingdom. Revelation 20 places the Great White Throne after the thousand years and describes the dead being judged according to their works before the final state. Taken together, these passages present multiple divine judgments that must be identified by the features Scripture assigns to each rather than combined into one general judgment.
32: The study examines Covenant Theology and Dispensational Theology as organizing frameworks that seek to explain how Scripture’s covenants, promises, peoples, administrations, and prophetic expectations relate across the biblical record. Covenant Theology emphasizes the unity of God’s redemptive purpose through theological covenant structures and commonly stresses continuity among God’s redeemed people, while Dispensational Theology emphasizes progressive revelation, distinguishable divine administrations, and continuing distinctions between Israel and the Church. Progressive Dispensationalism and New Covenant Theology revise elements of those major systems, while other approaches considered in the study do not necessarily function as complete macro-frameworks. The biblical passages examined identify covenant recipients, national and territorial promises, the Davidic throne, Israel’s Kingdom expectation, Paul’s distinct calling, and the Mystery made known through him. The Acts passages further record Paul’s calling while Israel’s prophetic ministry continues, followed later by the national pronouncement at Acts 28. Taken together, the evidence shows that theological frameworks must remain accountable to the audiences, covenants, promises, commissions, and revelatory distinctions actually stated in Scripture rather than determining those categories in advance.
33: The passages examined use crown language for several distinct purposes rather than presenting one uniform category of Christian reward. Paul uses crown imagery in connection with disciplined service, ministry fruit, faithful completion, and Christ’s future evaluation (1 Corinthians 9:24–27; 1 Thessalonians 2:19–20; Philippians 4:1; 2 Timothy 4:6–8). James 1:12 speaks of the crown of life within its stated twelve-tribe audience, Revelation 2:10 promises the crown of life to faithful sufferers at Smyrna, and 1 Peter 5:1–4 promises an unfading crown of glory to faithful elders when the Chief Shepherd appears. Revelation also portrays crowned elders without identifying them beyond what the vision states, while other passages use crowns for conquest, honor, beauty, corporate imagery, delegated authority, worship, and royal supremacy. Scripture does not itself collect these passages into an inspired five-crown system applicable without distinction to every believer. Taken together, these passages require each crown to be interpreted according to its stated recipient, setting, condition, timing, and purpose rather than by crown terminology alone.
34: The passages examined distinguish being filled with the Holy Spirit from receiving the Spirit, Spirit baptism, indwelling, sealing, manifestation, and the abiding description of a person as full of the Spirit. Acts 2:4 and Acts 4:31 record the same believing company being filled on separate occasions, with Acts 4 connecting renewed filling to prayer and bold proclamation rather than to repeated salvation or repeated reception of the Spirit. Luke also describes Stephen as full of the Spirit, Saul as being filled in Acts 9, Paul as filled before confronting Elymas, and the disciples at Pisidian Antioch as filled with joy and the Holy Spirit, while Acts 8, 10, and 19 use different Spirit-language for the events recorded there. Paul later describes believers as sealed with the Spirit after believing and separately commands them to “be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13–14; 5:18). Taken together, these passages present filling as Spirit-governed enablement or fullness expressed in particular moments and in the believer’s walk, while distinguishing it from the accomplished realities of receiving, possessing, and being sealed with the Spirit.
35: Study 35: Who Is the Israel of God?

The passages examined continue to use Israel, Jew, Gentile, remnant, and the Body as meaningful and distinguishable categories in Paul’s writings. Romans 2:17–3:1 addresses the Jew and distinguishes outward circumcision from inward reality without eliminating the continuing category of the Jew, while Romans 9–11 identifies Israel, a believing remnant within Israel, and Gentile participants without renaming the Gentiles Israel. Galatians 3:26–29 establishes equal standing in Christ and identifies those belonging to Christ as Abraham’s seed and heirs according to promise, but it does not call the Body Israel. Galatians 6:15–16 places “the Israel of God” after Paul’s new-creation rule, and the surrounding letter preserves the distinction between Paul’s uncircumcision ministry and the circumcision ministry recognized in Galatians 2:7–9. Ephesians 2:14–16 describes believing Jew and Gentile being reconciled in one Body and created as one new man rather than naming that new creation Israel. Taken together, these passages present “the Israel of God” as believing Israelites within Israel’s identified setting, while Paul’s corporate designation for believing Jew and Gentile together is the one Body and one new man in Christ.
36: Study 36: Jews, Gentiles, and the Church of God

The passages examined show Paul continuing to use Jews, Gentiles, and the Church of God as meaningful categories while also teaching equal standing and corporate unity in Christ. First Corinthians 10:32 names all three within Paul’s practical instruction concerning liberty, conscience, God’s glory, and avoiding unnecessary offense. Romans continues to identify Jews and Gentiles while placing both under sin and presenting justification through faith, and Paul can still identify himself historically as an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin (Romans 11:1). First Corinthians 12:13 states that Jews and Gentiles are baptized by one Spirit into one Body, while Ephesians 2:11–16 recalls the Gentiles’ former separation from Israel and then describes Christ creating Jew and Gentile as one new man and reconciling both to God in one Body. These passages distinguish historical or national origin from the new corporate standing created in Christ. Taken together, Paul’s threefold terminology preserves recognizable Jewish, Gentile, and Church categories while his one-Body teaching establishes equal standing and a new corporate unity in Christ without making those categories interchangeable
37: Study 37: What Does Paul Mean by New Creation?

The passages examined define Paul’s new-creation language from the believer’s position in Christ rather than from moral improvement, circumcision, or human achievement. Second Corinthians 5:17 states that the person “in Christ” is a new creation and places that statement within Christ’s representative death, resurrection, reconciliation, and God’s action toward those reconciled through Him (2 Corinthians 5:14–21). Galatians 6:15 likewise sets new creation against both circumcision and uncircumcision as grounds of standing. Ephesians 2:15–16 adds the corporate dimension by describing Christ creating one new man and reconciling both Jew and Gentile to God in one Body. Paul nevertheless distinguishes this accomplished standing from continuing renewal and future bodily transformation, speaking of the inward person being renewed, the mind being transformed, and the body still awaiting redemption and glorification (2 Corinthians 4:16; Romans 8:23; 12:2; Philippians 3:20–21). Taken together, these passages present new creation as God’s accomplished work establishing a new standing and corporate identity in Christ, from which continuing renewal proceeds and whose bodily completion remains future.
38: Study 38: Why Acts Is Not a Universal Experience Manual

The passages examined show Acts recording inspired history through events involving different audiences, commissions, purposes, and apostolic settings rather than prescribing one repeating experience for every believer. Pentecost, communal property, apostolic judgments, signs, healings, tongues, Spirit reception, repeated filling, visions, and direct guidance occur in identifiable circumstances, and the narrative does not turn their occurrence alone into a universal command. The sequences themselves vary: Acts 2, Acts 8, Acts 10, and Acts 19 do not present one identical order of Spirit reception and accompanying manifestations, while 1 Corinthians 12:29–30 expressly distinguishes spiritual functions rather than assigning every manifestation to every believer. Second Corinthians 12:12 associates signs with apostolic authentication, and Ephesians 1:13–14 describes believers as sealed with the Spirit after believing the gospel. Acts also records Peter’s prophetic ministry and Paul’s distinct apostleship operating concurrently during Acts 9–28, requiring each event to be read according to its own audience and commission. Taken together, these passages present Acts as authoritative and doctrinally instructive history whose events must be interpreted from their stated settings, while present obligation requires textual warrant beyond the fact that an event occurred.
39: Study 39: The Church’s Relationship to Israel’s Scriptures

The passages examined establish both the continuing authority of Israel’s Scriptures and the importance of preserving their original audiences, covenants, conditions, and promised outcomes. Second Timothy 3:14–17 identifies all Scripture as God-breathed and profitable, Romans 15:4 states that earlier writings were written for learning, and 1 Corinthians 10:1–13 uses Israel’s historical experience as admonition for Paul’s readers without identifying those readers as the Israel that experienced the Exodus. The worked passages preserve the same distinction: the Sabbath is identified as a sign involving Israel, Deuteronomy 28 addresses national covenant blessing and curse, Jeremiah 29 concerns Judah’s exiles and their restoration, and Malachi 3 addresses Israel’s tithing obligations, while Paul gives the Body its own instructions concerning days, prayer, giving, faith, and conduct. Paul can therefore draw instruction, warning, hope, testimony to Christ, and principles of faith from Israel’s Scriptures without transferring every original covenant obligation or promise to his audience. Taken together, these passages present Israel’s Scriptures as inspired and profitable for the Body while requiring present application to preserve the original claim and to follow the textual route by which Scripture itself establishes its application.
40: The passages examined use Abrahamic seed language in several related but distinguishable ways that must be determined from each argument. Genesis traces Abraham’s descendants and the selected covenant line while also promising blessing to the nations. Romans 4 appeals to Abraham’s justification before circumcision to establish righteousness by faith for believing circumcised and uncircumcised people, whereas Romans 9 uses Isaac and Jacob to explain God’s selected line within Paul’s argument concerning Israel. In Galatians 3, Paul identifies Christ as the decisive Seed to whom the promise points, states that the nations are blessed through faith, connects Abraham’s blessing with receiving the promised Spirit, and then calls those who belong to Christ Abraham’s seed and heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:8–16, 29). Galatians 4 further describes believers as sons and heirs through Christ, while Galatians 5 rejects circumcision as the condition of their standing. None of these passages requires every occurrence of “seed” to carry every feature of Abraham’s covenant or states that believing Gentiles thereby become Israel. Taken together, these passages present Christ as the decisive Seed and believers in Christ as Abraham’s seed in the relation Paul expressly establishes through faith, promise, the Spirit, and heirship, while Israel’s national covenant identity and territorial promises remain distinct questions governed by their own passages.
41: Study 41: Kingdom of God or Kingdom of Heaven?

The passages examined show that “kingdom of heaven” and “kingdom of God” are not two different kingdoms in the Gospel accounts. Matthew’s parallels with Mark and Luke use the two expressions for the same sayings and parables, while Matthew 19:23–24 uses both expressions successively for the same act of entering the Kingdom. Daniel supplies the prophetic background: the God of heaven establishes a Kingdom that exercises dominion under heaven and over earthly kingdoms (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14, 27). The Gospel accounts identify that Kingdom with Israel’s promised Davidic hope, including David’s throne, the house of Jacob, and the restoration of the Kingdom to Israel (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 1:6–7). At the same time, “kingdom of God” has a broader biblical range and can describe God’s sovereign reign beyond that particular prophetic Kingdom, while Paul also speaks of the Lord’s heavenly Kingdom in connection with his own hope (2 Timothy 4:18). Taken together, these passages present “kingdom of heaven” and “kingdom of God” as interchangeable descriptions of Israel’s promised Kingdom where the Gospel contexts identify that Kingdom, without making every occurrence of “kingdom of God” identical in scope or transferring Israel’s earthly Kingdom to the Body’s heavenly calling.
42: The passages examined show that baptism language must be defined by its agent, element, recipients, and result rather than automatically identified with water. Scripture speaks of Israel being baptized unto Moses, Christ’s baptism of suffering, John’s water baptism to manifest Messiah to Israel, and the Spirit’s baptism of believers into one Body (1 Corinthians 10:1–2; Luke 12:50; John 1:31; 1 Corinthians 12:13). Water baptism belongs prominently to Israel’s prophetic and Kingdom setting and continues historically throughout Acts, including during Paul’s ministry. Paul nevertheless distinguishes his commission from that of the Twelve by stating that Christ sent him “not to baptize, but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17). When Paul explains the Body’s baptism, he identifies the Spirit as the agent and the one Body as the result, while Romans 6 and Colossians 2 describe identification with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:11–12). Ephesians 4:3–6 then places “one baptism” among the unities belonging to the one Body. Taken together, these passages present the Body’s one baptism as the Spirit’s completed work of identifying every believer with Christ and placing the believer into the one Body, rather than water baptism as a requirement of Paul’s commission.
43: Study 43: The Gospel of the Grace of God

The passages examined define Paul’s gospel by its source, content, terms, audience, and results. Paul identifies God as its author, Christ as its subject, grace as its character, and himself as the steward to whom it was entrusted (Romans 1:1, 9, 16; Acts 20:24; 1 Timothy 1:11). First Corinthians 15:1–4 states its central content: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures. Romans 3:21–26 explains that God’s righteousness is received through faith apart from the Law and rests upon Christ’s redemptive and propitiatory work, while Romans 4 and Ephesians 2 exclude human works as the basis of acceptance. Those who believe are justified, reconciled, sealed with the Spirit, and placed into the one Body (Romans 5:1, 11; Ephesians 1:13–14; 1 Corinthians 12:13). Romans 16:25–26 relates this gospel to the revelation of the Mystery without making the gospel and the Mystery identical. Taken together, these passages present the gospel of the grace of God as the good news of Christ’s finished work for sinners, received by faith apart from human merit, through which believers receive their standing in Christ and entrance into the one Body.
44: The passages examined present walking in the Spirit as the believer’s ongoing response to the Spirit who already indwells those who belong to Christ. Galatians 5:16–18 describes a continuing conflict between the flesh and the Spirit and commands believers to walk in the Spirit rather than attempting to overcome the flesh through law or self-effort. The same chapter contrasts the manifest works of the flesh with the fruit produced by the Spirit and grounds the believer’s present walk in the positional fact that those belonging to Christ have crucified the flesh (Galatians 5:19–25). Romans 8:1–14 supplies the corresponding foundation: there is no condemnation for those in Christ, the Spirit indwells those who belong to Him, believers owe nothing to the flesh, and those led by the Spirit are identified as sons of God. Paul’s letters therefore describe the Spirit’s ministry to the Body through indwelling, sealing, leading, illumination, and fruit, while Acts records additional Spirit activity within its own historical and apostolic settings. Taken together, these passages present walking in the Spirit as a continuing life of dependence upon the indwelling Spirit, proceeding from the believer’s established position in Christ rather than functioning as the means of obtaining or preserving that position.
