45: The passages examined use sanctification language for related but distinguishable realities in the believer’s standing, conduct, and growth. First Corinthians identifies believers as already sanctified in Christ and places sanctification alongside righteousness, redemption, washing, and justification as an accomplished reality (1 Corinthians 1:2, 30; 6:11). First Thessalonians 4:3–7 then uses sanctification in connection with commanded conduct, calling those already belonging to God to live consistently with that standing, while Romans 6:19, 22 describes holiness as the fruit of a yielded life. Second Corinthians 3:18 adds the continuing dimension of transformation as believers are changed by the Spirit. These truths therefore distinguish completed positional sanctification from practical holiness and continuing spiritual transformation without separating them from one another. Israel’s holiness under the Mosaic covenant uses related language but rests upon Israel’s covenant relationship and its revealed statutes, whereas the Body’s sanctification rests upon union with Christ and instruction under grace. Taken together, these passages present sanctification under Grace as an accomplished standing in Christ that grounds a holy walk and continuing Spirit-worked transformation, rather than a standing progressively earned through human performance.
46: The passages examined ground the believer’s security in God’s accomplished work rather than in the believer’s ability to maintain an unbroken record of faithfulness. Ephesians states that believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit after believing and that the seal remains “unto the day of redemption,” while the Spirit is also identified as the earnest of the promised inheritance (Ephesians 1:13–14; 4:30). Romans 8:28–39 traces God’s action from foreknowledge to glorification and concludes with the declaration that nothing named can separate believers from the love of God in Christ. Second Timothy 2:11–13 distinguishes the question of reigning from God’s continuing faithfulness, while 1 Corinthians 3:11–15 explicitly describes a believer suffering loss of reward while the believer himself remains saved. Paul’s conditional statements must therefore be interpreted according to their individual arguments rather than treated as a single formula for revoking salvation. Romans 6:1–2 also rejects the conclusion that security gives believers permission to continue in sin. Taken together, these passages present the believer’s standing as secured by Christ’s finished work, the Spirit’s seal, and God’s own faithfulness, while preserving genuine accountability for conduct, service, and reward.
47: The passages examined present giving under Grace as a willing response to God’s grace rather than as the continuation of Israel’s covenant tithe. Second Corinthians 8–9 begins with believers giving themselves to the Lord, describes Paul’s appeal as “not by commandment,” and measures acceptable giving according to a willing mind and what the giver actually possesses (2 Corinthians 8:5, 8, 10–12). Christ’s self-giving provides the pattern, equality of care provides an objective, responsible administration protects the collection, and each giver is to purpose freely rather than give grudgingly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 8:9, 13–24; 9:7). First Corinthians 16:1–2 gives an orderly pattern for setting resources aside, while Philippians 4:10–19 presents giving as fellowship and partnership in gospel ministry. Israel’s tithe, by contrast, belonged to the Mosaic covenant and was connected with Israel’s land and Levitical priesthood (Leviticus 27:30; Numbers 18:21–24; Malachi 3:8–10). Taken together, these passages present giving under Grace as voluntary, purposeful, proportionate, accountable, and Christ-centered generosity that flows from grace already received rather than from a prescribed covenant percentage or a promise of proportional material return.
48: The passages examined place Paul’s household instructions within the larger context of a Spirit-filled life and a standing already secured in Christ. Ephesians 5:21 introduces mutual submission before Paul addresses the individual relationships that follow. Wives are instructed concerning submission to their own husbands, while husbands are commanded to love with the self-giving standard of Christ’s love for the Church (Ephesians 5:22–33). Children are told to obey and honor, while fathers are instructed to nurture without provoking them to wrath (Ephesians 6:1–4). Servants are directed to serve as unto Christ, while masters are reminded that they themselves answer to a Master in heaven who shows no partiality (Ephesians 6:5–9; Colossians 3:22–4:1). First Timothy 5:8 adds the responsibility of providing for one’s own household. These instructions establish genuine order while simultaneously placing every relational responsibility under accountability to the Lord. Taken together, these passages present the Christian household as an ordered community governed by mutual submission, self-giving love, obedience, nurture, provision, justice, and accountability to Christ, without making household function a measure of greater or lesser standing before God.
49: The passages examined present resurrection as an ordered series of events grounded in the accomplished resurrection of Christ rather than as one undifferentiated future event. First Corinthians 15:20–23 identifies Christ as the firstfruits and explicitly speaks of an order and an “afterward.” Paul describes the Body’s own hope as the dead in Christ rising, living believers being caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air, and all being changed from mortality to immortality (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; 1 Corinthians 15:51–54). Prophetic passages describe resurrection in connection with Israel’s Kingdom hope, while Revelation 20 distinguishes those raised to reign with Christ from the dead who do not live again until the thousand years are finished (Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:4–6). Revelation 20:11–15 then places the later resurrection in connection with the Great White Throne. Ezekiel 37 must be distinguished from these bodily resurrection passages because the text itself identifies the dry bones as the whole house of Israel and describes restoration to Israel’s land. Taken together, these passages present distinct resurrection events with different companies, timing, and destinies, all resting upon the certainty established by Christ’s resurrection as firstfruits.
50: The passages examined show that election language must be interpreted by identifying whom God chooses, the stated basis of the choice, its setting, and its appointed destiny. Deuteronomy 7:6–8 presents Israel as God’s chosen nation and grounds that election in His sovereign love and oath to the fathers rather than Israel’s size or merit. Romans 9 traces God’s purpose through the selected line of Isaac and Jacob, while Romans 11 identifies a believing remnant within Israel and affirms that God’s gifts and calling concerning Israel remain irrevocable (Romans 9:6–13; 11:1–7, 28–29). Ephesians 1:3–6 presents the Body’s election differently, locating it “in Christ” before the foundation of the world, while 2 Thessalonians 2:13–14 connects believers’ participation with belief of the truth and calling through the gospel. Both elections originate in God rather than human merit, but their stated objects, historical settings, and destinies are not interchangeable. Taken together, these passages present Israel’s national election and the Body’s election in Christ as distinct expressions of God’s sovereign purpose, requiring the word “elect” to be interpreted according to the audience and purpose of each passage rather than used to merge the two programs.
51: The passages examined distinguish the physical covenant sign given to Abraham and carried forward in Israel from the spiritual reality Paul describes for believers in Christ. Genesis 17:9–14 identifies circumcision in the flesh as the covenant token given to Abraham and his household, while Leviticus 12:3 carries that physical rite into Israel’s life under the Law. Deuteronomy 10:16 and Jeremiah 4:4 use circumcision language of Israel’s heart, and Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that the LORD will perform that inward work in Israel. Acts 15 rejects the demand that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved, while Timothy’s circumcision for Jewish access and Titus’s refusal under doctrinal pressure show that the physical act and its imposed necessity are different questions (Acts 16:1–3; Galatians 2:3–5). Paul states that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision determines standing in Christ and describes believers as having a circumcision “made without hands,” joined with their identification with Christ in burial and resurrection (Galatians 5:6; 6:15; Colossians 2:11–13). Taken together, these passages present fleshly circumcision as the covenant sign given in Abraham’s line and maintained within Israel, while the circumcision Paul describes for believers in Christ is a non-fleshly work of God that does not require or redefine Abraham’s physical sign.
52: The passages examined use sonship and adoption language in distinguishable settings and identify both present possession and future manifestation. Exodus 4:22 calls Israel God’s son and firstborn in connection with the Exodus, and Romans 9:4 lists “the adoption” among the possessions Paul attributes to Israelites. Galatians 4:4–7 describes redemption from under the Law followed by the reception of adoption and the Spirit’s cry of “Abba, Father,” while Ephesians 1:4–5 places the adoption Paul describes there within God’s purpose in Christ before the foundation of the world. Romans 8:15–17 states that believers have received the Spirit of adoption, that the Spirit bears witness that they are children of God, and that children are heirs. Romans 8:23 then speaks of believers still waiting for “the adoption,” immediately identifying it as “the redemption of our body,” so the future statement does not erase the adoption already described as received. Taken together, these passages present Israel’s national adoption in its own covenant and historical setting and the believer’s adoption in Christ as a present sonship confirmed by the Spirit, with the redemption of the body remaining its future manifestation.
53: The passages examined use redemption language for deliverance while requiring each passage to identify the company, bondage, means, and timing involved. Exodus 6:6 describes God redeeming Israel from Egyptian bondage with a stretched-out arm and great judgments, while Isaiah 59:20 looks forward to the Redeemer coming to Zion and Romans 11:26–27 applies that prophetic expectation to Israel and Jacob. Paul describes believers as presently possessing redemption through Christ and specifically connects that redemption with His blood and the forgiveness of sins (Romans 3:24; Ephesians 1:7; Colossians 1:14). Other passages likewise identify Christ’s self-giving and blood as the price of redemption and describe His offering as sufficient and unrepeated (Titus 2:14; Hebrews 9:12; 10:11–14). Yet Ephesians 1:13–14 speaks of the future redemption of the purchased possession, and Romans 8:23 identifies the redemption of the body as still awaited. Taken together, these passages present redemption according to the bondage, deliverance, company, and means each text identifies, while presenting the believer’s redemption in Christ as already possessed through His accomplished work and awaiting its future bodily completion.
54: The passages examined present justification as God’s declaration of righteous standing and consistently distinguish its ground from the means by which that verdict is received. Romans 3:20 states that no flesh is justified by deeds of the Law, while Romans 3:24–28 describes justification as freely given by grace through the redemption in Christ and received by faith apart from deeds of the Law. Romans 4:25 associates justification with Christ’s death and resurrection, and Romans 5:1 states the resulting peace with God for those justified by faith. Paul explains Israel’s failure in Romans 9:30–10:4 not as insufficient zeal, but as seeking righteousness through works rather than submitting to God’s righteousness in Christ. Galatians 2:16 repeatedly excludes works of the Law from justification, while Abraham’s righteousness in Genesis 15:6, examined by Paul in Romans 4, was counted to him through belief before circumcision and centuries before the Mosaic Law. Taken together, these passages present justification as God’s righteous verdict grounded in Christ’s accomplished work and received by faith rather than human works, a pattern Paul traces to Abraham rather than a principle first created with his own ministry.
55: The passages examined present reconciliation as God’s work in Christ addressing estrangement and establishing peace. Romans 5 describes those now reconciled as formerly enemies and states that justified believers have peace with God through Jesus Christ and have received reconciliation through Him (Romans 5:1, 10–11). Second Corinthians 5:18–21 identifies God as the initiator of reconciliation in Christ, distinguishes that accomplished work from the word and ministry entrusted to its messengers, and follows the announcement with the appeal, “be ye reconciled to God.” Ephesians 2:13–18 describes Christ making peace between Jew and Gentile, reconciling both to God in one Body through the cross, and giving both access to the Father by one Spirit. Colossians 1:20–23 speaks broadly of reconciliation through the blood of Christ’s cross and then directly addresses readers who had been alienated but were reconciled through His death. The broad language of “world” and “all things” does not itself state that every individual already possesses the reconciled standing described of those who receive it. Taken together, these passages present reconciliation as God’s initiative in Christ that answers enmity with peace, is proclaimed through an entrusted message, and becomes the received possession of those whom Paul describes as reconciled to God.
56: The passages examined show that inheritance language does not identify one undifferentiated possession but must be defined by its giver, heir, object, basis, and timing. Genesis identifies the land as a specific inheritance promised to Abraham’s descendants through the covenant line, while later passages distinguish that grant from Israel’s tenure, exile, and promised restoration in the land (Genesis 12:7; 15:7–21; 17:7–8; Deuteronomy 30:1–5). The same biblical vocabulary can also name other kinds of inheritance, including the LORD Himself as the priestly portion, demonstrating that the word alone does not determine its object (Numbers 18:20). Paul develops heirship in relation to Christ, faith, adoption, the Spirit, and the believer’s standing in Him, while Ephesians speaks of inheritance together with the Spirit as its earnest and of Gentiles as fellow heirs in the same Body (Galatians 3–4; Romans 8:14–17; Ephesians 1:11–14; 3:6). First Peter 1:3–4 likewise describes an inheritance reserved in heaven, showing that heavenly custody does not by itself identify every feature of the inheritance or its corporate setting. Taken together, these passages require each inheritance to retain the recipients and possession Scripture assigns to it: Israel’s promised land remains a stated covenant inheritance, while Paul describes believers in Christ as heirs whose inheritance is secured in relation to Christ and guaranteed by the Spirit.
57: Study 57: The Eternal Purpose of God

The passages examined distinguish what God purposed before the ages from the time at which He disclosed particular parts of that purpose. Ephesians 1:9–11 places God’s will and purpose in Christ and looks toward the fullness of times in which all things in heaven and earth are gathered together in Him, while Ephesians 1:22–23 separately identifies the Church as Christ’s Body under His headship. Ephesians 3 states that the Mystery was made known to Paul by revelation, identifies its same-Body content, describes it as previously hidden in God, and states that God’s manifold wisdom is now made known through the Church to principalities and powers in heavenly places (Ephesians 3:3–10). Paul then identifies this present work as according to God’s eternal purpose in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:11). Second Timothy 1:9–10 likewise distinguishes purpose and grace given in Christ before the world began from their later manifestation, while other Pauline passages preserve the same pattern of prior purpose followed by disclosure in time. Taken together, these passages present God’s eternal purpose as centered in Christ, including a Mystery previously hidden and subsequently revealed, with the Church presently displaying God’s wisdom while Christ’s ultimate headship embraces the larger ordering of things in heaven and earth.
58: The passages examined use dispensation or stewardship language for an entrusted administration or responsibility whose content must be learned from its surrounding context. First Corinthians 9:16–18 describes Paul’s preaching as a necessity laid upon him and a dispensation committed to him, establishing responsibility and accountability rather than defining a chronological period. Ephesians 3:1–9 identifies the dispensation of God’s grace as given to Paul for Gentile readers, connects it with revelation of the Mystery, and states its same-Body content. Colossians 1:24–29 similarly describes Paul’s ministry as a stewardship given to him for others and connects that stewardship with making known the previously hidden Mystery. Ephesians 1:9–10 uses related administrative language for the future fullness of times, showing that the same term can describe different arrangements whose actor, content, recipients, and timing are supplied by their respective passages. The word therefore does not by itself establish a particular number of biblical eras, a method of salvation, or the complete content of the administration it names. Taken together, these passages present a dispensation as an entrusted or ordered administration defined by the responsibility being administered, with Paul’s distinctive stewardship identified through the revelation and ministry specifically committed to him.
59: Study 59: The Law’s Jurisdiction and the Body of Christ

The passages examined identify the Mosaic Law as a covenant given to a named people and distinguish its original jurisdiction from its continuing value as inspired Scripture. Exodus 19 addresses the house of Jacob and children of Israel, while Deuteronomy recalls that the covenant was made with Israel at Horeb and identifies its commandments as covenant obligations (Exodus 19:3–8; Deuteronomy 4:13; 5:1–3). Paul likewise identifies Israel with “the covenants” and “the giving of the law” and states that the Law exposes sin without providing justification or life (Romans 3:19–20; 9:4; Galatians 3:21). Romans 6–7 describes believers as not under the Law and as released from its jurisdiction through union with Christ, while simultaneously rejecting sin as the consequence of that release. Paul then supplies positive instruction for the Body through the Lord’s authority, the Spirit, love, and the commands given in his letters, including conduct that may correspond morally with earlier commandments without placing the Body under the Sinai covenant. Taken together, these passages present the Mosaic Law as Israel’s covenant administration and present the Body as serving God under the authority of Christ and grace, free from Sinai’s covenant jurisdiction without being free from righteousness, obedience, or the continuing instruction of Scripture.
60: Study 60: The Churches Named in Scripture

The passages examined show that the word church or assembly does not by itself identify one corporate people in every occurrence. Acts 7:38 uses the term for Israel assembled in the wilderness, while Matthew 16:18 and 18:17 use assembly language within Jesus’ earthly ministry without supplying Paul’s later definition of the one Body. Acts identifies real assemblies at Jerusalem before Paul’s calling and continues to speak of churches in Judaea, Galilee, Samaria, and elsewhere, with their immediate historical settings supplying their identity (Acts 5:11; 8:1; 9:31; 12:5). Paul’s later description of the churches he had persecuted as “churches of God” or assemblies “in Christ” establishes their genuine relationship to God and Christ without, by those expressions alone, defining them as the one Body whose membership Paul explains elsewhere. When Paul explicitly describes the Body, he identifies believers as incorporated by one Spirit into one Body and presents Jew and Gentile as reconciled to God in that one Body under Christ as Head (1 Corinthians 12:12–13; Ephesians 1:22–23; 2:14–16; 3:6). Taken together, these passages establish that ekklesia identifies an assembly, while the assembly’s specific corporate identity must be determined from its speaker, audience, setting, commission, and explicit doctrinal description rather than from the shared word church alone.
61: The passages examined place Revelation 12 within Israel’s prophetic setting and identify its figures through imagery and descriptions supplied by the chapter and its scriptural background. The woman bears the sun, moon, and twelve stars, imagery rooted in Jacob’s family in Genesis 37:9–11, while Isaiah 66:7–8 supplies the picture of travailing Zion. Revelation 12:9 explicitly identifies the dragon as the old serpent, the Devil, and Satan, while the ten horns correspond with the prophetic imagery of Daniel 7. The male child is caught up to God and His throne, and the study connects that description with the 144,000 later shown with the Lamb as Israel’s firstfruits company (Revelation 12:5; 14:1–5). The woman is preserved for 1,260 days, also expressed as “a time, and times, and half a time,” and Daniel 12:7 places corresponding language within the experience of the holy people. The chapter then moves from war in heaven to the dragon’s persecution of the woman and finally to war against the remnant of her seed, who keep God’s commandments and have the testimony of Jesus Christ (Revelation 12:7–17). Taken together, these passages present Revelation 12 as a prophetic account concerning Israel, Satan’s opposition, the protected firstfruits company identified in the study as the 144,000, and the wider believing remnant that remains under persecution.
62: The passages examined place Matthew 5:17–20 within Jesus’ Kingdom proclamation to disciples in Israel while the Mosaic Law remained in force. Jesus explicitly denies that He came to destroy the Law or the Prophets and states instead that He came to fulfil them (Matthew 5:17). Matthew’s use of “fulfil” elsewhere describes Scripture brought to its intended realization, while “the law and the prophets” functions as a comprehensive designation for Israel’s Scriptures. Verse 18 states that not one jot or tittle will pass from the Law until the stated conditions are fulfilled, and verses 19–20 connect obedience, teaching, righteousness, standing in the Kingdom, and entrance into it. Paul later addresses believers in a different revealed setting and states that they are not under the Law, that the Law’s custodial role reaches its appointed boundary, and that Christ has addressed the Law’s governing relationship in connection with the one new man (Romans 6:14; Galatians 3:23–25; Ephesians 2:15). Taken together, these passages present Matthew 5:17–20 as Christ’s affirmation of the Law and Prophets within Israel’s Kingdom setting, while Paul’s later instruction establishes that the Body’s relationship to God is not governed by the Mosaic covenant.
63: The passages examined place the sign of Isaiah 7:13–16 within the crisis confronting the house of David during the reign of Ahaz while also preserving Matthew’s later identification of its fulfillment in Jesus. Isaiah addresses the house of David after Ahaz refuses the offered sign, and the Lord then announces a sign involving the virgin, conception, a son, and the name Immanuel (Isaiah 7:10–14). Verses 15–16 attach an immediate historical horizon to the sign by stating that before the child reaches the described stage of discernment, the land of the two threatening kings will be forsaken. Isaiah continues the Immanuel language beyond chapter 7 and develops the Davidic and royal expectation through chapters 8–11. Matthew 1:18–25 explicitly returns to Isaiah 7:14 in the account of Jesus’ conception and states that the event occurred to fulfil what the Lord had spoken through the prophet, while Luke 1:26–35 independently connects Jesus’ birth with David’s house and throne. Taken together, these passages present Isaiah 7:13–16 as a sign given to David’s house with a historical horizon in Ahaz’s crisis and a Messianic fulfillment explicitly identified by Matthew in the birth of Jesus Christ.
64: Study 64: The Wedding and the Wedding Supper

The passages examined distinguish the marriage of the Lamb, His wife, and those called to the marriage supper while locating the scene within Revelation’s prophetic sequence. Revelation 19:7–8 announces that the marriage of the Lamb has come, speaks of “his wife” in the third person, and states that fine linen was granted to her. Israel’s prophetic Scriptures repeatedly use marital imagery in describing the LORD’s relationship with Israel, while Revelation 21:2, 9–14 identifies the Lamb’s wife with the holy city and places the names of Israel’s twelve tribes upon its gates. Revelation 19:9 then pronounces blessing upon those “called” to the marriage supper, grammatically distinguishing the invited company from the wife already described in verses 7–8. The Gospel accounts likewise distinguish bridegroom, bride, friends, and invited guests in their respective wedding and banquet settings, while prophetic and Gospel passages connect banquet imagery with the Kingdom. Paul’s use of marriage imagery concerning believers serves his stated comparisons without itself announcing the wedding or identifying its guest list. Taken together, these passages present the Lamb’s wife and those called to the marriage supper as distinguishable participants within the prophetic wedding scene rather than as interchangeable designations for the same company.
65: The passages examined identify Acts 2:42 as a report of what the Jerusalem converts continued in following Peter’s Pentecost message rather than as an independent statement defining doctrine for every later assembly. Acts identifies Peter standing with the Eleven and repeatedly names his audience as Judaea, Jerusalem, Israel, and ultimately “all the house of Israel” (Acts 2:14, 22, 36). Those who received Peter’s word were baptized and then continued steadfastly in the apostles’ doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers (Acts 2:41–42). The teaching recorded in Acts 2–5 continues to concern Jesus as Israel’s risen Messiah, Israel’s repentance, prophetic fulfillment, and the promised restoration, while the believers’ communal practices occur within that same Jerusalem setting. Galatians 2:7–9 later distinguishes responsibilities committed to Peter and Paul, and Paul identifies the doctrine and Mystery entrusted to him through revelation. Paul’s letters separately instruct the Body concerning teaching, fellowship, prayer, giving, and the Lord’s Supper. Taken together, these passages present Acts 2:42 as the steadfast practice of Jerusalem believers under the Twelve’s apostolic teaching, while the Body’s doctrinal instruction is established in the revelation and teaching committed through Paul.
66: The passages examined identify Matthew 28:18–20 as a commission spoken by the risen Christ to the Eleven within the Kingdom setting developed throughout Matthew. Matthew explicitly names the eleven disciples as those gathered on the appointed mountain in Galilee, and Jesus grounds their assignment in the authority given to Him in heaven and earth (Matthew 28:16–18). The commission centers upon making disciples of all nations, accompanied by going, baptizing, and teaching them to observe what Christ had commanded the Eleven. Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8 further identify Jerusalem as the starting point of their expanding witness, while Matthew’s own uses of “the end of the age” connect that expression with the prophetic consummation associated with the Son of Man’s coming. Paul later states that his gospel came through revelation of Jesus Christ, identifies a distinct stewardship of the Mystery, and records recognition of distinguishable apostolic responsibilities in Galatians 2:7–9. Second Corinthians 5:18–20 separately describes the ministry of reconciliation entrusted in Paul’s ministry. Taken together, these passages present Matthew 28:18–20 as the risen King’s commission to the Eleven, while Paul’s later revelation identifies a distinguishable commission and ministry associated with the Body of Christ.
67: The passages examined present Melchizedek first as a historical king-priest and later as the scriptural pattern used to explain Christ’s superior priesthood. Genesis 14:18–20 identifies Melchizedek as king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, records his blessing of Abram and reception of a tithe, but supplies no genealogy or explanation for the bread and wine. Psalm 110:1–4 later joins royal and priestly language by declaring under divine oath that David’s Lord will be “a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews develops that connection by describing Melchizedek as “made like unto the Son of God,” reasoning from Genesis’ recorded silence rather than explicitly identifying Melchizedek as Christ (Hebrews 7:1–3). Hebrews then uses Abraham’s tithe and Melchizedek’s blessing to establish the superiority of that order to Levi and states that a change in priesthood entails a corresponding change in law (Hebrews 7:4–12). The argument culminates in Christ’s enduring priesthood established by divine oath rather than Levitical descent. Taken together, these passages present Melchizedek as the king-priest whose scriptural portrayal provides the pattern through which Hebrews explains the superiority, permanence, and oath-established character of Christ’s priesthood.
68: The passages examined use several forms of written-register language and require each reference to be interpreted according to its own name, audience, and setting. Israel’s Scriptures speak of those written among the living in Jerusalem, the writing of the house of Israel, those counted in Zion, and a book of remembrance, without identifying all these registers as one book (Isaiah 4:3; Ezekiel 13:9; Psalm 87:6; Malachi 3:16). Exodus 32:32–33 and Psalm 69:28 contain blotting-out language but do not call their respective books the Book of Life. Daniel 12:1 speaks of Daniel’s people being delivered during the time of trouble, everyone found written in the book. Jesus tells the seventy that their names are written in heaven, while Paul states that his fellow laborers’ names are in the Book of Life (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3). Revelation 3:5 promises the overcomer that his name will not be blotted out, while Revelation 20:11–15 distinguishes the books associated with works from “another book,” the Book of Life. Taken together, these passages present divine records of names in several settings and the Book of Life as a distinct record in Revelation’s final judgment scene, while the texts themselves do not authorize treating every biblical register as the same book or every reference to blotting out as the same event.
69: The passages examined preserve distinguishable earthly and heavenly settings within the final ordering of all things under Christ. Isaiah 65:17–25 and 66:22 describe new heavens and a new earth in connection with Jerusalem, the LORD’s people, their seed, and earthly conditions, while Psalm 37:29 and Matthew 5:5 likewise speak of inheriting the land or earth. Revelation 21:1–4 presents the new heaven and new earth with God dwelling among people, and the New Jerusalem bears the names of Israel’s twelve tribes upon its gates and the twelve apostles of the Lamb upon its foundations (Revelation 21:9–14). Paul, by contrast, describes believers as blessed and seated in heavenly places, possessing heavenly citizenship and a hope laid up in heaven (Ephesians 1:3; 2:6; Philippians 3:20; Colossians 1:5; 3:1–4). Ephesians 1:10 and Colossians 1:16–20 speak broadly of things in heaven and things on earth brought under Christ without describing those spheres as becoming one location or one corporate identity. Taken together, these passages present an earthly realm associated with Israel’s stated prophetic inheritance and a heavenly position and hope described for the Body, with both remaining distinguishable under the universal headship of Christ in God’s final order
70: Study 70: Born of Water and of the Spirit

The passages examined place Jesus’ words about being born of water and Spirit within His conversation with Nicodemus, whom John identifies as a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, and whom Jesus addresses as “the teacher of Israel” (John 3:1, 10). Jesus states that a person must be born anew or from above to see the Kingdom and must be born “of water and of the Spirit” to enter it (John 3:3–5). Nicodemus initially understands the language as a second physical birth, but Jesus contrasts flesh with Spirit and rebukes him for not understanding what, as Israel’s teacher, he should have known (John 3:4–10). Within Israel’s Scriptures, Isaiah 44:3 and Ezekiel 36:25–27 associate water and Spirit with divine cleansing, renewal, and restoration, while Ezekiel 37 combines Spirit or breath with Israel’s restoration imagery. Jesus continues the conversation with additional material drawn from Israel’s Scriptures, including the lifted serpent of Numbers 21 (John 3:14–15). First Corinthians 12:13 later describes the Spirit’s baptism into the one Body in a different audience and setting. Taken together, these passages present the birth of water and Spirit in John 3 as the cleansing and Spirit-wrought renewal Jesus expected a teacher of Israel to recognize from Israel’s prophetic Scriptures, in connection with seeing and entering the promised Kingdom.
71: The passages examined present the genealogies of Matthew and Luke as distinct but complementary claims concerning Jesus’ descent and His relationship to Israel’s promises. Matthew opens by identifying Jesus Christ as the son of David and the son of Abraham, then traces a deliberately arranged line from Abraham through David and the royal succession to Joseph, while changing the established formula at Matthew 1:16 to identify Mary as the one from whom Jesus was born. Luke places his genealogy at the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry, qualifies His relationship to Joseph with “as was supposed,” traces the line through David’s son Nathan rather than Solomon, and continues through Abraham to Adam (Luke 3:23–38). Both lists establish Davidic and Abrahamic descent while following different names after David, and neither Gospel explicitly explains every difference between them. Jeremiah 22:24–30 pronounces judgment upon Coniah and his seed concerning prosperity upon David’s throne, while Matthew nevertheless records Jeconiah within the royal genealogy and presents Jesus as born of Mary rather than begotten by Joseph. Taken together, these passages present the two genealogies as textual witnesses to Jesus’ place within the Abrahamic and Davidic lines required by Israel’s Messianic promises, while preserving the distinctive structure and claims each Gospel gives its own genealogy.
72: The passages examined distinguish the setting in which Jesus gives the bread and cup to the Twelve from Paul’s later instruction concerning the Lord’s Supper at Corinth. Luke and Matthew place the original meal at Passover with the Twelve and connect the bread and cup with Christ’s body, His shed blood, the New Covenant, forgiveness, and the coming Kingdom (Luke 22:14–20; Matthew 26:26–29). Jeremiah 31:31–34 identifies the New Covenant itself with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Paul states that he received from the Lord what he delivered to the Corinthians and instructs them to eat the bread and drink the cup in remembrance of Christ, thereby proclaiming the Lord’s death until He comes (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). His correction of the Corinthian disorder requires self-examination, proper regard for the Lord’s body, and conduct consistent with the Supper they profess to observe (1 Corinthians 11:27–34). Paul does not state that participation in the Supper makes the Corinthians parties to the covenant named in Jeremiah. Taken together, these passages present the Lord’s Supper for the Body as a remembrance of Christ and a proclamation of His death until He comes, using the bread and cup Paul states that he received from the Lord and delivered to the Corinthian assembly.
73: The passages examined present the Davidic Covenant as God’s sworn promise concerning David’s house, seed, throne, and Kingdom. Second Samuel 7 begins with David’s desire to build a house for the LORD, but God responds by promising to make David a house, raise up his seed after him, establish his Kingdom, and establish the throne of that Kingdom forever (2 Samuel 7:8–16). The immediate promise includes a son who can be chastened for iniquity, while the enduring promise extends beyond any single sinful descendant to David’s continuing house and throne. Psalms 89 and 132 describe the promise as an oath and covenant, preserving the sworn commitment even while acknowledging discipline upon David’s descendants. The prophets continue the expectation through language concerning David’s Branch, shepherd, prince, King, people, land, and restored rule. The New Testament identifies Jesus with David’s promised line, and Peter states that God had sworn to David concerning the fruit of his body and his throne (Acts 2:29–36). Taken together, these passages present the Davidic Covenant as God’s enduring commitment to David concerning his dynastic house, promised descendant, throne, and Kingdom, with the New Testament identifying Jesus Christ as the Davidic heir in whom the promise reaches its Messianic focus.
74: The passages examined describe several end-time rulers and opponents with overlapping features while requiring each passage to retain its own names and claims. Second Thessalonians 2 identifies “the man of sin,” “the son of perdition,” and “that Wicked,” who exalts himself above what is called God, sits in the temple of God, operates with Satanic power, signs, and lying wonders, and is ultimately destroyed by the Lord at His coming (2 Thessalonians 2:3–10). The same passage refers to a restraining influence with both neuter and masculine language but does not identify the restrainer (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7). Daniel describes rulers who exalt themselves, oppose God, afflict the holy people, participate in desolating events, and operate within stated prophetic periods, while Revelation 13 describes a beast possessing blasphemous authority and receiving worship. John’s letters separately use the term “antichrist” for those who deny the Father and the Son and also speak of “many antichrists” already present (1 John 2:18–22). The passages share significant features, but none explicitly states that every title in Daniel, Paul, Revelation, and John names the same individual. Taken together, these passages present a recurring prophetic pattern of opposition, blasphemy, deception, persecution, and final divine judgment while requiring the identification of the man of sin, Daniel’s rulers, Revelation’s beast, and John’s antichrist terminology to remain within what each text explicitly establishes.
75: The passages examined present faith before the Cross as belief in what God had revealed to particular people within their own historical settings. Abraham believes God’s promise concerning his seed, and that faith is counted to him for righteousness (Genesis 15:5–6). Israel is said to believe after hearing God’s words and seeing His signs, while later unbelief is described as refusing to believe the words and signs already given (Exodus 4:30–31; 14:31; Numbers 14:11; Psalm 106:12, 24). Hebrews 11 likewise describes faith through the particular words, promises, warnings, and expectations received by Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and others, while stating that these witnesses did not receive the completed promise during their lifetimes. Before the Cross, the disciples confess Jesus as Messiah, yet passages such as Luke 18:31–34 explicitly state that they did not understand His predictions concerning His coming death and resurrection. After the resurrection, Jesus opens the Scriptures and explains what Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had said concerning Him (Luke 24:25–27, 44–47). Taken together, these passages present faith before the Cross as believing and responding to the revelation God had actually given at that time, without requiring the believer to possess knowledge that the text itself says had not yet been understood.
76: The passages examined present Ephesians 6:10–20 as a call for believers to stand in strength supplied by the Lord against explicitly identified spiritual opposition. Paul commands his readers to be strong “in the Lord, and in the power of his might” and to put on the whole armour of God so that they may stand against the wiles of the devil (Ephesians 6:10–11). He states that the struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities, powers, rulers of the darkness of this world, and spiritual wickedness in heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12). The armour consists of truth, righteousness, preparation associated with the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God, with the verbs of the passage emphasizing putting on, taking, standing, withstanding, praying, and watching. Isaiah and 1 Thessalonians contain related armour imagery, but each passage assigns its imagery within its own setting. Paul closes not with a command to attack or exercise independent authority over the spiritual powers, but with persevering prayer for all saints and for boldness in his own proclamation (Ephesians 6:18–20). Taken together, these passages present the armour of God as God-given provision by which believers stand firm in the Lord against spiritual opposition through truth, righteousness, faith, salvation, the word of God, watchfulness, and prayer.
77: The passages examined present Romans 13:1–7 as instruction concerning the believer’s relationship to governing authorities and the obligations Paul explicitly names. Paul commands every soul to be subject to the higher powers and states that the powers that exist are ordained of God (Romans 13:1–2). He describes the ruler as God’s minister in connection with good and evil, identifies wrath and the bearing of the sword within that governmental function, and gives conscience as an additional reason for subjection (Romans 13:3–5). The passage then names what is owed: tribute, custom, fear, and honour (Romans 13:6–7). The surrounding context tells believers not to avenge themselves and to live peaceably, while other passages likewise address submission, prayer for rulers, and proper honour (Romans 12:17–21; Titus 3:1; 1 Timothy 2:1–2; 1 Peter 2:13–17). Acts 4:19 and 5:29 record apostolic refusal where obedience to human authority conflicts with obedience to God, but Romans 13 itself does not attempt to define every circumstance in which such conflict may arise. Taken together, these passages present the believer as subject to governing authority, obligated to render what is due and to maintain a conscience toward God, while preserving God as the believer’s ultimate authority.
78: Study 78: The Sabbath and Its Meanings

The passages examined give the Sabbath several related meanings while consistently requiring its audience and setting to be preserved. Genesis 2 records God resting on, blessing, and sanctifying the seventh day but does not record a Sabbath command to Adam. Exodus 16 first names the Sabbath in connection with Israel, and the Sinai passages command its observance, ground it in both creation and Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, and explicitly identify it as a sign between the LORD and the children of Israel (Exodus 20:8–11; 31:12–17; Deuteronomy 5:12–15). Israel’s Law and Prophets continue to treat Sabbath observance within that covenantal setting, while Jesus addresses Sabbath controversies during His earthly ministry among Israel. Acts records synagogue activity on Sabbath days without making those narrative occurrences a Sabbath command for the Body. Paul later states that believers are not to be judged concerning a sabbath day and treats the esteeming of particular days as a matter not to be imposed upon another believer (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17). Hebrews 4 develops the theme of God’s rest within its own argument without redefining the seventh-day sign given to Israel. Taken together, these passages present the seventh-day Sabbath as a sign and covenant observance expressly given to Israel, while later Scripture draws instruction from the themes of day and rest without transferring Israel’s Sabbath command to the Body of Christ.
79: Study 79: The Realms of the Dead

The passages examined use several terms concerning death, the dead, judgment, and final punishment that should not be collapsed into a single undifferentiated place. The Old Testament uses Sheol in passages translated “grave,” “hell,” and “pit,” describing descent to the dead while also speaking in differing ways about those found there. The New Testament uses Hades in passages including Luke 16 and Acts 2, where Peter’s quotation of Psalm 16 uses Hades for the Sheol named in the Psalm. Gehenna appears in the Gospels in warnings of judgment and carries its own textual and historical setting, while Revelation distinguishes Hades from the lake of fire by stating that Death and Hades are themselves ultimately cast into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:13–15). Second Peter 2:4 uses a separate term in describing sinning angels being cast down and reserved unto judgment, while other passages use the imagery of the deep or abyss in their own settings. Paul’s letters speak of death and of being with Christ without using those expressions to redefine every term found elsewhere. Taken together, these passages present Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, the place of confinement described in 2 Peter, and the lake of fire through distinguishable settings and descriptions, requiring each term to retain the meaning and function supplied by its own passage.
80: The passages examined distinguish what God purposed before the foundation of the world from what occurred and was manifested within history. First Peter 1:18–21 identifies Christ as a lamb without blemish and without spot and states that He was “foreordained before the foundation of the world” but “manifest in these last times.” The verse therefore joins foreordination with the time before the world’s foundation and manifestation with a later historical time. Other passages use “before,” “from,” or “since” the foundation of the world in connection with different subjects, including the Father’s love for the Son, God’s choosing, a prepared Kingdom, finished works, shed blood, and written names; the shared phrase does not make all those statements identical. Revelation 13:8 and 17:8 associate the foundation-of-the-world language with the Lamb and the book of life, while their syntax requires careful reading rather than supplying a conclusion from the phrase alone. Scripture traces lamb imagery through Genesis, Exodus, Isaiah, John, Acts, and Paul, while Hebrews 9:26 explicitly places Christ’s sacrificial suffering in His historical appearing rather than as a repeated event since the world’s foundation. Taken together, these passages present Christ the Lamb as foreordained within God’s purpose before the foundation of the world and manifested in history to accomplish His sacrificial work, preserving the distinction between divine purpose established beforehand and its execution in time.
81: The passages examined use several distinct expressions concerning the Spirit, prayer, and tongues rather than defining them as one practice. Romans 8:26–27 states that believers do not know what they should pray for as they ought and that the Spirit Himself makes intercession for the saints with groanings that cannot be uttered, according to the will of God. Ephesians 6:18 commands believers to pray always with all prayer and supplication “in the Spirit,” with watchfulness, perseverance, and supplication for all saints, while Jude 20 separately speaks of “praying in the Holy Ghost.” First Corinthians 14 distinguishes praying in a tongue, praying with the spirit, praying with the understanding, and speaking in an assembly where interpretation and edification govern the use of tongues. Acts 2, 10, and 19 record people speaking with tongues, but those accounts do not describe the speech as prayer. Taken together, these passages present the Spirit as helping and interceding in prayer and direct believers to pray in the Spirit, while the passages concerning tongues retain their own wording and settings and do not make praying in the Spirit synonymous with praying or speaking in tongues.
82: The passages examined define the kinsman-redeemer from the law before later uses of the redeemer language are considered. Leviticus 25 places redemption within Israel’s law concerning land, poverty, family possession, and personal freedom, identifying a near relative who may redeem property or a person sold into service and requiring the appropriate redemption price. Ruth places that law into narrative form: Boaz is identified as a near kinsman, acknowledges that another kinsman is nearer, proceeds publicly before witnesses, and acts after the nearer relative declines (Ruth 2:20; 3:9–13; 4:1–10). Other passages use the same redeemer terminology in distinguishable settings: Numbers 35 for the avenger of blood, Job for the living Redeemer, and Isaiah repeatedly for the LORD as Israel’s Redeemer. Psalm 49 establishes a further boundary by stating that no ordinary brother can redeem another from death. Hebrews 2:14–17 states that Christ partook of flesh and blood, was made like His brethren, and through death acted concerning death and deliverance, but the passage does not itself call Him the kinsman-redeemer or explicitly map every requirement of Leviticus 25 onto Him. Taken together, these passages present the kinsman-redeemer as a near relative authorized and able to act for another within the specific redemption provisions Scripture gives, while later redeemer passages must be connected to that legal pattern only where their own wording establishes the connection.
83: The passages examined present 1 Corinthians 7 as Paul’s ordered response to questions concerning marriage, singleness, mixed marriages, present circumstances, and remaining in one’s calling. Paul begins by addressing mutual marital duty, temporary abstinence by consent, and the unmarried and widows, while distinguishing permission from command and acknowledging differing gifts (1 Corinthians 7:1–9). To the married he gives a command he attributes to the Lord concerning separation and reconciliation, while to believers married to unbelievers he gives further instruction under the marker “I, not the Lord” and tells the believing spouse not to leave when the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain (1 Corinthians 7:10–16). Verses 17–24 repeatedly instruct readers to abide in the calling in which they were called, illustrated by circumcision and servitude. Concerning virgins, Paul expressly states that he has no commandment of the Lord and gives his judgment, explaining his counsel in light of the “present distress” and the statement that “the time is short” (1 Corinthians 7:25–38). The chapter closes by binding marriage while a spouse lives, permitting remarriage after death “only in the Lord,” and again identifying Paul’s judgment as such (1 Corinthians 7:39–40). Taken together, these passages present marriage and singleness as matters addressed through specific instructions, permissions, judgments, circumstances, and audience markers that must be retained rather than flattened into one universal formula
84: The passages examined place present suffering beside future glory without treating every statement about suffering as a description of every believer’s identical experience. Romans 8 identifies believers as children and heirs, speaks of suffering with Christ and being glorified together, and declares that the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that will be revealed (Romans 8:17–18). The passage widens to creation’s groaning and the believer’s waiting for the redemption of the body, then speaks of the Spirit’s help, God’s purpose, justification, and glorification before naming tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, and sword (Romans 8:19–39). Paul concludes that none of the things named can separate believers from the love of God in Christ. Second Corinthians 4 speaks more specifically from Paul’s ministry setting, describing treasure in earthen vessels, trouble and persecution, the dying of the Lord Jesus borne in the body, and the contrast between the outward person perishing and the inward person being renewed. Paul then sets “our light affliction, which is but for a moment” beside “a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:16–18). Taken together, these passages present suffering as belonging to the present experience described in their respective settings while directing attention toward future glory, bodily redemption, resurrection hope, inward renewal, and the unbroken love of God in Christ.
85: Study 85: The World Guilty Before God

The passages examined develop Paul’s charge of universal guilt through a sequence of distinct addresses rather than through one undifferentiated accusation. Romans 1:18–32 speaks of people who suppress truth in unrighteousness, describes what God made manifest, declares them without excuse, records their exchange of God’s glory and truth, and three times states that God gave them up or over. Romans 2 then turns to the person who judges another, declares God’s judgment impartial, distinguishes those who sin without the Law from those who sin in the Law, and speaks of Gentiles who do not have the Law while their conscience bears witness (Romans 2:1–16). Paul next addresses the person “called a Jew,” names circumcision and possession of the Law, and states that the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God (Romans 2:17–3:8). Romans 3:9 then brings the argument together by charging both Jews and Gentiles as “all under sin,” supports that charge with written Scripture, and concludes that every mouth is stopped, all the world becomes guilty before God, and no flesh is justified by deeds of the Law (Romans 3:9–20). Taken together, these passages bring Gentile, moral judge, Jew, and ultimately the whole world under the charge of sin and accountability before God, preparing for the change in argument introduced by “But now” in Romans 3:21.
86: The passages examined use “servant” for more than one identified or described figure and therefore require each occurrence to be read within its own immediate setting. Isaiah explicitly calls Israel and Jacob God’s servant in numerous passages, describing that servant as chosen, formed, remembered, redeemed, and at times blind and deaf (Isaiah 41:8–9; 42:19; 44:1–2, 21; 48:20). Isaiah 42:1–9 introduces an unnamed servant upheld by the LORD, endowed with His Spirit, bringing judgment to the Gentiles, and given as a covenant of the people and a light of the Gentiles. Isaiah 49:1–7 contains the striking statement “Thou art my servant, O Israel” while also describing that servant as acting to bring Jacob and Israel back to God, and Isaiah 50 presents a speaking servant who hears, obeys, suffers, and trusts the LORD. Isaiah 52:13–53:12 describes the LORD’s servant as exalted, rejected, wounded, bearing sins, dying, and afterward seeing the result of His work. New Testament writers then explicitly apply particular servant texts to Jesus, including Matthew’s use of Isaiah 42 and Acts 8’s identification of the suffering figure in Isaiah 53 with Jesus. Taken together, these passages present servant language in Isaiah with both expressly named and unnamed referents, while the New Testament explicitly identifies Jesus with particular servant passages without requiring every occurrence of “servant” in Isaiah 41–53 to have the same immediate referent.
87: The passages examined show that “the last days,” “the latter days,” and related expressions are used in multiple settings and cannot be assigned one uniform meaning merely because similar time-language appears. Genesis 49 places “the last days” within Jacob’s words concerning what will befall his sons, while Numbers 24 and Deuteronomy 4 and 31 use “the latter days” in statements involving Israel and other named peoples. Isaiah 2 and Micah 4 use “the last days” in nearly parallel descriptions involving the LORD’s house, Zion, Jerusalem, the nations, and the end of war, while Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Daniel use later-day language within their own prophetic settings. Peter introduces Joel’s prophecy at Pentecost with “in the last days” and applies its wording to the events he is explaining in Acts 2. Hebrews states that God “hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son,” while James, Peter, John, Jude, and Paul employ last-day, last-time, or latter-time expressions in letters addressed to their own readers and concerning different circumstances. No single passage states that every occurrence of these expressions names one identical chronological period. Taken together, these passages present last-days terminology as context-dependent time language whose referent must be established from the speaker, audience, events, and promises of each passage rather than assumed from the phrase alone.
88: Second Corinthians 6:14–7:1 addresses the Corinthian assembly’s fellowship with unbelievers and calls believers to separation from associations that join what belongs to God with what stands opposed to Him. Paul develops that command through five contrasts, culminating in the incompatibility of the temple of God with idols, and identifies the Corinthians themselves as the temple of the living God. He then draws language from Leviticus 26, Ezekiel 37, Isaiah 52, and 2 Samuel 7, each arising from its own setting in Israel’s Scriptures, and applies that scriptural language to his appeal for separation, cleansing, and holiness. The passage does not identify marriage, business, friendship, or ordinary contact with unbelievers as the unequal yoke itself, nor does it state that the Corinthian assembly has entered Israel’s covenants, land, kingdom, or national identity. Taken on its own terms, the passage calls believers to reject fellowship incompatible with their identification with God and to pursue holiness in the fear of God.
